title: The Akal Takht today
hook: the rebuilt Takht faces the Harmandir across the causeway

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Harmandir's day: prakash at dawn, hymns all day, and the Granth carried to rest at night. Your line was carried to rest. What did you put away with care last night? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

Stand on the marble at the edge of the pool in Amritsar and turn slowly. In front of you, out on the water at the end of the causeway, the Harmandir Sahib, low and gold, full of singing. Behind you, on dry land, a tall white building with a gold dome, rising above the courtyard. You can't look at both at once. You have to turn. Last night's palki crossed between them. Today we stay with the second building, as it stands now, and with the line that runs between the two.
screen: `TURN SLOWLY ON THE MARBLE.` → `ONE ON THE WATER, ONE ON LAND.` → `YOU HAVE TO TURN.`

segments.voice: First, the building you see today. The Akal Takht you see today has been rebuilt. This path told that story on an earlier day: after the building was wrecked, Sikhs insisted on raising it again by their own hands, as kar seva. So the Takht standing now is new stone on old ground. The place, Sikhs say, is what carries the authority. Second, the line. Tradition says Guru Hargobind raised his seat facing the Harmandir. Walk the causeway back from the Harmandir, through the gateway at its end, and the Takht stands just beyond. The two face each other across the courtyard. One stands in the water, the other is raised on land. Third, what each one does. In the Harmandir, the Guru's hymns are sung from before dawn into the night. From the Akal Takht, the panth's decisions are made and its letters go out, as you heard on an earlier day. One is for listening. One is for answering. Neither has its back to the other. That's today's line: facing each other. Fourth, the name over the second door. The opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib describe God as akaal moorat, here in paraphrase: a form beyond time. Akal, the Timeless. So the building that deals with worldly things, quarrels and rulings and the panth's business, carries the name of what is beyond time. Every night the Granth makes the crossing between them, the word carried across to where the decisions are made. A visitor only has to turn around on the marble to see what that crossing is for.
screen: `NEW STONE ON OLD GROUND.` · `ONE ON THE WATER, ONE RAISED ON LAND.` · `ONE FOR LISTENING, ONE FOR ANSWERING.` · `AKAL: THE TIMELESS.` · then, large: `FACING EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the two buildings. Settle, and breathe. See the Harmandir in front of you, low and gold on the water. Breathe in, and listen for the singing. Now turn, slowly, and see the Akal Takht behind you, raised and white. Breathe out, and think of one decision waiting for you this week. Turn back to the water. Turn back to the Takht. Let the two face each other inside you. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The Akal Takht today. The rebuilt throne of the Timeless at Amritsar, raised on land and facing the Harmandir across the courtyard. Today's word.

Your line: facing each other. Today, before you make one decision, stop and turn toward whatever helps you listen first: a line, a silence, a person you trust. Then decide. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Pilgrims at Amritsar visit both the Harmandir Sahib and the Akal Takht, which face each other across the courtyard; the Guru Granth Sahib rests at the Akal Takht complex at night and returns to the Harmandir at dawn.
